requirement: REL-1 — the physical two-machine demonstration; the viewer's broadcast freshness within 5 seconds
method: The browser's DOM carries a MutationObserver installed on the viewer's message list; it records the wall-clock instant each message card FIRST appears (a per-sequence set, so a catch-up page is recorded once and a live SSE frame is recorded at its arrival). The sender records the instant the server acknowledged its send (the api-client's own clock, immediately after the committed answer). The difference is the viewer's freshness.

same_clock_measurement.why: the sender and the viewer are the SAME machine (NSG-Mac-mini.local), so the difference carries NO clock-skew term at all
same_clock_measurement.sender: CLAUDE-MAC-1 (the Mac installation of the frozen portable package)
same_clock_measurement.verdict: pass — 0.107 s against the 5 s bound
same_clock_measurement.endpoints: the measured interval runs from the sender's HTTP acknowledgement of the committed send to the instant the viewer's MutationObserver sees the message card inserted into the DOM. It does NOT run from send-start to the first painted pixel: the acknowledgement is after the commit, and the MutationObserver callback fires before the paint. This is an operational proxy for the viewer's freshness, not a general end-to-end latency SLA (release-gate review, Vex).

cross_machine_measurement.why: the sender is the OTHER physical machine (ngs-staging), so the two clocks differ; the offset is measured, not assumed
cross_machine_measurement.sender: CLAUDE-STAGING-1 (the staging installation of the frozen Claude Code package)
cross_machine_measurement.clock_offset_method: the server's HTTP Date header is the common reference: 9 samples per client, the median of (client midpoint - server epoch). The header has 1-second resolution, so each median carries about +/-450 ms of quantization uncertainty.
cross_machine_measurement.reported_as: 0.217 s (the corrected cross-machine freshness). The arithmetic: elapsed = (viewer_clock - mac_offset) - (sender_clock - staging_offset) = raw_difference + (staging_offset - mac_offset) = 102 + 115 = 217 ms. The first version of this file subtracted the offset in the wrong direction; the release-gate review (agy, Sally) caught it and this is the corrected value.
cross_machine_measurement.verdict: pass - 0.217 s corrected (raw 0.102 s) against the 5 s bound, with a +/-0.9 s clock-offset uncertainty
cross_machine_measurement.uncertainty: each clock offset is the median of 9 samples of (client midpoint - the server's HTTP Date); the Date header has 1-second resolution, so each median carries roughly +/-450 ms of quantization uncertainty, and the DIFFERENCE of the two medians inherits up to about +/-900 ms from that term alone, before any network asymmetry. The nine raw samples and the capture code were not retained, so this is not a calibrated total bound. The verdict does not depend on it: even at the worst case the measurement is about 1.1 s, far inside the 5 s bound.
cross_machine_measurement.endpoints: the measured interval runs from the sender's HTTP acknowledgement of the committed send to the instant the viewer's MutationObserver sees the message card inserted into the DOM. It does NOT run from send-start to the first painted pixel: the acknowledgement is after the commit, and the MutationObserver callback fires before the paint. This is an operational proxy for the viewer's freshness, not a general end-to-end latency SLA (release-gate review, Vex).

honest_limits: The measured interval is sender-acknowledgement -> DOM card insertion, not send-start -> painted pixel. The acknowledgement is after the commit and the observer fires before the paint, so the interval is not the whole user-perceived latency.

The cross-machine number carries the clock-offset uncertainty stated above (each offset median has about +/-450 ms of quantization; their difference up to about +/-900 ms). The same-clock number carries no clock term at all.

Only seq 7 and seq 8 are live SSE arrivals; seq 1-6 entered the DOM as the page's initial catch-up page (the observer was attached after those messages were already committed), so their timestamps are the catch-up instant and NOT latencies.
Two canary measurements were taken per path; the earlier pair (seq 2 and seq 3) gave 120 ms and 113 ms raw - the same order of magnitude, so the result is not a single lucky sample.
